prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and opening new regimes of precision measurement

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case on the shortlist of a new measurement capability that changes what physics can observe. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift, and the first strontium lattice demonstrations followed. Ye's group then pushed systematic uncertainty and coherence to the 10^-18 level, with the comb link to the optical frequency. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE), and clock comparisons across sites are routine. That is the reproducibility I look for. It is already used for relativistic geodesy at centimetre height differences, for bounds on varying constants and for dark-matter searches, and the redefinition of the second rests on it. The attribution is clean, with a proposer-demonstrator and a record-setter, and it fits the two-name credited set exactly.
statement.case_against: The honest reservation is novelty against earlier prizes. Hall and Hansch (2005, combs) and Wineland (2012, ion control and ion clocks) sit close by, so a committee could read lattice clocks as the natural continuation of a decorated programme. The scientific payoff so far is mostly tighter limits and a better instrument, not a new fact about nature, and the redefinition of the second has not happened yet. Credit is also spread over groups not on the credited list (NIST ion clocks, SYRTE, PTB, JILA colleagues such as Ludlow and Hinkley), and my knowledge of the detailed priority history is from memory.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks Bloch, Greiner and Zoller first for optical-lattice quantum simulation, because it turned textbook many-body models into controllable laboratory systems, and ranks Katori and Ye second while worrying that the clocks may be seen as technology rather than discovery.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-technology worry seriously, but I think it applies more strongly to B020 than to B024. The clocks give a single, quantitative, repeatedly confirmed number (10^-18) and a first-principles design idea. The quantum-simulation programme is still working toward its headline question, the doped Hubbard model and pseudogap physics, and it overlaps with the 2001 prize on condensates and the 2012 and 2022 quantum prizes. I agree the physics is strong and I keep B020 as my first alternative. I would choose Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger over the Zoller trio, because the observed Mott transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and microscopes are what experiments established, while Jaksch and Zoller's proposal is hard to separate from Cirac and Zoller's role elsewhere. On the 2005 and 2012 overlap, I would say those prizes rewarded the comb and ion control, and the lattice clock is the distinct step that made 10^-18 accessible.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino detection first as a detector-driven discovery that opens a new observational window, and places the lattice clocks third as a precision achievement with strong multi-laboratory confirmation.
responses.response: I share his instrument-first criterion, and I accept that IceCube opens a window onto the universe in a literal sense. My concern is attribution. Only Halzen is credited, and a prize for a cubic-kilometre detector with a very large collaboration that omits the people who built and operated it would be hard to defend, as Pearce himself notes. A lone laureate also has to carry both the AMANDA concept and the 2013 detection. Source identification beyond TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 is still at modest significance. For the clocks the repeated confirmation across independent laboratories is complete today, so I see less risk there. I would like to hear whether he thinks neutrino astronomy has crossed the threshold from first detection to an established field.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first for the theory-experiment tie between Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and gives lattice clocks seventh place over the closeness to the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: The theory-plus-experiment tie in B021 is attractive and the field has been confirmed by many groups. My reservation is the unresolved pairing mechanism and the large sample-to-sample dependence on twist-angle disorder, which he also lists. In an experimental sense the correlated insulator and superconductivity are established, but the interpretation is still moving and the field is about eight years old. I also note that his seventh place for the clocks rests on closeness to the 2005 prize. I think that overstates the overlap. The comb provided a ruler. The lattice clock is a different atomic system and a different concept, designed to cancel the trapping shift, and it is the reason clocks now reach 10^-18. I would be happy to see B021 recognised later, once the pairing question has settled.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture underlying superconducting quantum processors, but notes that Girvin's role against Blais is an allocation problem, that the 2025 prize may make the field look already recognised, and that he cannot claim full neutrality.
responses.response: I rank B002 fifth, and I agree on the science: strong coupling, dispersive readout and the transmon rest on the 2004 work, and it has been very widely replicated. My hesitation is timing. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is recent, and a second circuit prize so soon invites a charge of repetition. I would also point out that the Blais against Girvin choice for the theory slot is a real weakness in the three-name set, and I do not think the committee should resolve it by default. I appreciate his disclosure of his own closeness to the field. I count it as a reason to weigh his ranking as informed but not independent evidence, and as a reason to keep B002 as an alternative but not the lead.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues judge optical lattice clocks sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and whether the committee wants to wait for the redefinition of the second.

Exact allocation between Katori's conception and first demonstration and Ye's precision and systematics achievements, and whether other lattice-clock groups would need to be considered. I have not independently verified the priority history.
Whether a discovery-about-nature prize would be preferred over a measurement-instrument prize in a year when B020 or B021 could be framed as new states of matter.
How the committee should treat the overlap in credited names (Cirac, Zoller) between B020 and B006.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict is apparent from my profile. Two connections are worth flagging for transparency. I spent a year of my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is a later JILA colleague of Hall's, so there is a distant scientific lineage to the candidate group, with no collaboration, shared funding or institutional tie to Katori or Ye that I know of. In addition, my own field, atomic physics and quantum optics at Lund, is close to several shortlisted ballots (B024, B020, B006, B002, B043), so I am not a neutral outsider on the AMO candidates.
